abstract:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) represents a malignant
tumor linked
to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) that is characterized by distinctive,
clinically relevant biological features. As protein N-glycosylation
plays critical roles in cancer progression, we applied quantitative
glycoproteomics to characterize NPC-specific glycosylation patterns.
Using label-free proteomics and intact N-glycoproteomics, we analyzed
17 NPC tissues and 7 normal mucosal epithelia. Integrated analysis
with PET/CT imaging and bioinformatics revealed correlations among
differentially expressed glycoproteins, glycosyltransferases, and
immunophenotypes. Functional validation demonstrated that MANEA, an
enzyme linked to high-mannose glycosylation, influences NPC cell proliferation
and migration. Furthermore, MANEA likely modulates PD-L1 expression
through high-mannose glycans. Our findings indicate that high-mannose
glycoproteins are predominant in NPC and may promote tumor progression
not only by enhancing malignant behavior but also by facilitating
immune escape via PD-L1 regulation, thereby impairing antitumor immunity.

Materials and Methods
Clinical Sample Acquisition
This study was conducted
after ethical approval (No: 2024-108) was granted by the Clinical
Research Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen
University. Written informed consent was acquired from all participants
preceding sample collection. The biopsy samples consisted of nasopharyngeal
tissues obtained via endoscopy from patients with diagnosed or suspected
NPC. Critically, all samples were collected prior to any therapeutic
intervention.
Sample Preparation
Frozen samples were removed from
−80 °C storage and immediately pulverized into a fine
powder using a mortar precooled with liquid nitrogen. Transferred
the ground powder to a preweighed centrifuge tube, and determined
the powder volume based on the occupied volume in the centrifuge tube.
Add four volumes of ice-cold lysis buffer (composed of 1% Triton X-100,
protease/phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (MedChemExpress), 50 μM
PR-619 (MedChemExpress), 3 μM Trichostatin A (TSA, MedChemExpress),
and 50 mM Nicotinamide (NAM, Sigma-Aldrich) to each sample group.
Among them, TSA (a histone deacetylase inhibitor) and NAM (a sirtuin
deacetylase inhibitor) are coadded to synergistically inhibit deacetylase
activity, thereby better stabilizing the acetylation modification
state of N-glycopeptides and avoiding artificial loss of modifications
during sample processing. Before the experiment, concentrated stock
solutions of all inhibitors were freshly prepared and diluted to the
desired final concentrations in lysis buffer. Immediately proceed
with ultrasonic lysis using a probe sonicator (300W, 3s pulse/10s
interval, total 5 min) while maintaining samples on ice to prevent
protein degradation. The lysate was subjected to centrifugation at
4 °C (12,000 ×
g
, 10 min). The supernatant
was then collected for subsequent protein concentration measurement
employing a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay. Normalize protein content,
adjust volume with lysis buffer, add equal and then 4-fold volumes
of prechilled acetone successively, and precipitate at −20
°C for 2h. After precipitation, centrifuge at 4500
g
for 5 min, discard the supernatant, wash the precipitate 2–3
times with prechilled acetone, air-dry, and resuspend in 200 mM TEAB.
Sonicate for complete dissolution. Digest proteins overnight with
trypsin (1:50 w/w), reduce disulfide bonds with 5 mM dithiothreitol
(DTT) at 37 °C for 60 min, and alkylate with 11 mM iodoacetamide
(IAA) in the dark at room temperature for 45 min.
PTM enrichment
for N-glycosylation: For glycopeptide enrichment, the supernatant
was loaded onto a hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC)
microcolumn (5 μm particles, 120 Å pore size; Welch). The
column was then centrifuged at 1000 ×
g
for
15 min. Subsequently, it was rinsed three times with washing buffer
to remove nonspecific binding.
Glycopeptides
were eluted sequentially with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid, 50 mM ammonium
bicarbonate, and 50% acetonitrile. Eluates were combined, lyophilized,
desalted using C18 ZipTips (according to the manufacturer’s
protocol), and lyophilized again for LC-MS/MS analysis (the initial
enrichment of intact N-glycopeptides was 200 μg peptides).
LC-MS/MS Analysis
For proteomic analysis: Tryptic peptides
were reconstituted in solvent A and injected onto a homemade reversed-phase
column (25 cm × 100 μm internal diameter [i.d.]). The mobile
phase consisted of solvent A (0.1% formic acid, 2% acetonitrile/in
water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid, 90% acetonitrile/in water).
Peptide separation was achieved using the following gradient program
on an EASY-nLC 1200 UPLC system (ThermoFisher Scientific) at a constant
flow rate of 500 nL/min: 0–68 min, 6–23% solvent B;
68–82 min, 23–32% solvent B; 82–86 min, 32–80%
solvent B; 86–90 min, 80% solvent B. The eluted peptides were
analyzed via an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer coupled with
a nanoelectrospray ion source. Separated peptides were analyzed on
an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (nanoelectrospray ion source, 2300 V; FAIMS
CV: −45 V, −65 V); Full MS scan: 400–1200
m
/
z
, 60,000 resolution; MS/MS scan: fixed
first mass 110
m
/
z
, 15,000 resolution,
TurboTMT off; top 25 precursors selected for MS/MS (20 s dynamic exclusion);
HCD fragmentation (NCE 27%); AGC target 100%, intensity threshold
50,000 ions/s, max injection time Auto (CV: compensate voltage; HCD:
Higher-energy Collisional Dissociation; NCE: Normalized collision
energy; AGC: Automatic gain control).
3D Mass Spectrometer
was used for N-glycoproteomic analysis: Tryptic
peptides were reconstituted in solvent A (0.1% formic acid [FA], 2%
acetonitrile [ACN]) and injected onto a homemade reversed-phase (RP)
analytical column (25 cm length, 75 μm i.d.]). Separation used
an EASY-nLC 1200 UPLC with a gradient: 5–25% B (0.1% FA in
90% ACN) for 60 min, 25–35% for 22 min, 35–80% for 4
min, 80% hold for 4 min, flow rate 450 nL/min. Analysis employed a
Q Exactive HF-X with nano-ESI at 2.0 kV. Full MS scans (350–1600
m
/
z
) were acquired at a resolution of 60,000.
A maximum of 20 precursor ions were selected for MS/MS analysis with
30 s dynamic exclusion. HCD fragmentation was conducted at NCE of
28%, and fragment ions were detected in the Orbitrap at a resolution
of 30,000. The instrument settings were as follows: fixed first mass
of 100
m
/
z
, AGC target of 1E5, intensity
threshold of 3.3E4, and maximum injection time of 60 ms.
Database Search
For proteomic analysis: MS/MS data
were processed via Proteome Discoverer (v.2.4) and searched against
Homo_sapiens_9606_SP_20230103.fasta (20389 entries), reverse decoy
and contaminants database. Trypsin (Full) was specified as cleavage
enzyme, up to 2 missing cleavages. Peptide criteria: min length 6,
max 3 modifications per peptide. Mass error: 10 ppm (precursor), 0.02
Da (fragment). Fixed modification: Cys carbamidomethylation. Variable
modifications: Met oxidation, protein N-terminal acetylation, Met
loss, Met loss + acetylation. FDR (protein/peptide/PSM) < 1% (PSM:
peptide-spectrum matches).
For N-glycoproteomic analysis: Raw
data were processed via MSFragger (v.3.4) and the tandem mass spectra
were searched against Homo_sapiens_9606_SP_20230103.fasta (20389 entries)
concatenated with reverse decoy database. Strict trypsin was specified
as cleavage enzyme, up to 2 missing cleavages. Peptide criteria: length
range 7–50. Fixed modification: Cys carbamidomethylation. Variable
modifications: protein N-terminal acetylation, Met oxidation. Set
mass offsets to the default list of glycosylated modifications. FDR
(protein/peptide/PSM) < 1%.
Data Quality Control, Quantification, and Differential Protein
Screening
Post-MS data acquisition, quality control (QC)
checks include peptide length/number, protein coverage, and molecular
weight distributions. Label-Free Quantification intensities (corrected
for intersample variation) are centralized to derive relative protein
quantities (
R
). Protein fold change (FC) was defined
as the ratio of mean
R
values across the comparison
groups. Significance testing uses
t
tests on log-transformed
R
values (default
p
< 0.05) to meet
normality assumptions.
Motif analysis of modified sites employed
MoMo (motif-x algorithm),
using identified
sites as 10-amino acid peptides (phosphorylation: ±6 aa) from
all putative modification sites within the species. A sequence pattern
was deemed a significant motif if ≥20 peptides supported it
and statistical testing yielded
p
< 0.000001.
Bioinformatics Methods
Proteins were annotated using
eggnog-mapper v2.0 for GO terms (Cellular Component, Molecular Function,
Biological Process) and KEGG pathways via BLASTp
,
­(
e
value ≤0.0001, top hit selected). Fisher’s
exact test (background: all identified proteins) determined enrichment
significance (
p
< 0.05).
For Gene Set Variation
Analysis (GSVA) enrichment scoring and clustering, we conducted GSVA
enrichment analysis on nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) samples using
a predefined set of immune cell-related genes. Subsequently, based
on the enrichment scores of individual immune cells derived from each
sample, hierarchical clustering was performed using the ‘hcluster’
package in R.
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was
employed to assess
the association between glycan types and protein expression, considering
r
> 0.3 as significant positive correlation. For strongly
correlated proteins, we applied linear regression in R to study the
link between glycosylation and expression, adjusting
p
-values with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Cytoscape (v3.9.1)
was utilized to construct interaction networks, using only models
with False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.01. Linear regression was also
used for intraprotein relationships.
All
regression analyses focused on differentially expressed intact glycopeptides
and peptides from tumor and normal tissues.
Imaging Histology Analysis
In terms of imaging histology,
we collected a total of 10 cases of nasopharyngeal cancer patients
who had completed glycosylation histology for their initial PET/CT.
The ROI region of CT nasopharyngeal cancer was manually outlined according
to the patients’ initial radiotherapy target area, and the
ROI region was downsampled (down sampling) to pet size (128 ×
128 × 299) using sitkNearestNeighbor. And the pet image histology
features were extracted using python 3.11, SimpleITK library and radiomics
and other libraries.
The extracted features
include First Order Statistics, shape based (2D, 3D), GLCM, GLSZM,
GLRLM, NGTDM, GLDM.
Cell Culture and Transfection
The human nasopharyngeal
undifferentiated squamous cell carcinoma cell lines HK1 and C666.1
were utilized in this study. HK1 cells were maintained in complete
RPMI-1640 medium (Bio-Channel, China) supplemented with 10% fetal
bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin solution. C666.1
cells were cultured in high-glucose complete DMEM (Bio-Channel, China)
containing 10% FBS and 1% (100×) penicillin-streptomycin (PS)
solution. Both cell lines were incubated at 37 °C in a humidified
cell culture incubator with 5% CO
2

si-MANEA#2:5′-CCCTAGAATAGCCAAGAATTA-3′;
si-MANBA#1:5′-CCAGGGAGATTTAGTGACAAT-3′;
si-MANBA#2:5′-CCAATCTACATCAAGGACTAT-3′;
si-EDEM3#1:5′-GCATTCAGATATTCCAGGTAA-3′;
si-EDEM3#2:5′-CCTTCTGAACAGACTTCTAAT-3′.

Total RNA was isolated from cells using the RNA Isolater Total RNA
Extraction Kit (LABLEAD, China). Complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized
with HiScript II qRT SuperMix for qPCR (LABLEAD, China), and expression
levels were detected via ChamQ SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Novoprotein,
China). All data were normalized to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
(GAPDH) as the internal reference gene. Tissue-derived data were quantified
using the 2
–ΔCt
method, while data from other
samples were calculated via the 2
–ΔΔCt
method. All primers were synthesized by Tsingke Biotechnology (Beijing,
China), with their sequences listed below:
MANEA-F: 5′-CGCGGTCTTAACCTCTCCTC-3′;
MANEA-R: 5′-TCCTTCTCCGAAACTTTGCCA-3′;
MANBA-F:
5′-GGGCCTGATCCAGGATTCTT-3′;
MANBA-R: 5′-TCCTTCTCCGAAACTTTGCCA
3′;
EDEM3-F: 5′-GCAGTGATACTGCCCCTCTG-3′;
EDEM3-R: 5′-ACCTTTTAATATTGCTGCTCGATCT-3′;
GAPDH-F:
5′-GGAGCGAGATCCCTCCAAAAT-3′;
GAPDH-R: 5′-GGCTGTTGTCATACTTCTCATGG-3′.
Wound Healing Assay
Cells were plated in 6-well plates
and subjected to transfection. After 48 h of incubation, the medium
was replaced with serum-free medium. A uniform scratch was generated
in each well using a sterile 200 μL pipet tip. Images were taken
at the same locations at 0 and 12 h (for HK1) or 0 and 24 h (for C666.1),
and the scratch width was measured.
CCK-8 Assay
Cell proliferation was assessed using a
CCK-8 assay. HK1 (800 cells/well) or C666-1 (2000 cells/well) cells
were seeded into 96-well plates. After cell attachment, CCK-8 reagent
(GLPBIO, USA) was added daily from day 0 to day 4. Following 1–4
h of incubation at 37 °C in the dark, the absorbance at 450 nm
was recorded using a microplate reader.

Statistical analysis of the experimental
results was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software, and data
were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Results
with
p
-value < 0.05 were defined as the threshold
for statistical significance: * (
P
< 0.05), **
(
P
< 0.01), *** (
P
< 0.001),
**** (
P
< 0.0001), and ns (no significant difference).

body:
Introduction
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), a rare
form of squamous cell carcinoma
originating from the nasopharynx epithelium, exhibits a higher prevalence
in southern China, Southeast Asia, the Arctic, North Africa, and the
Middle East.
−
The development of NPC has a multifactorial etiology,
among which EBV infection, genetic predisposition, environmental and
lifestyle habits are involved, among others.
,
Accumulating
evidence from prior studies indicates that dysregulated expression
of glycoproteins correlates strongly with the progression of NPC.
−
Thus, gaining insight into the molecular changes linked to the onset
and progression of NPC is essential for developing disease-specific
therapeutic strategies tailored to NPC patients.
We profiled
NPC via global proteomic analyses,
which
revealed how proteome-wide dysregulation remodels
specific protein interaction networks and activates oncogenic signaling
pathways. Glycoproteomics focuses on the investigation of glycans
and glycoproteins as well as their associated functions within living
organisms.
−
Glycosylation, which refers to the process where
glycans (either oligosaccharides or polysaccharides) are covalently
bonded to proteins, lipids, or other organic compounds, represents
a crucial post-translational modification that is prevalently present
in organisms.
−
In accordance with the disparities between glycans and the molecules
to which they attach, glycosylation can be principally categorized
into N-glycosylation, O-glycosylation, proteoglycans, glycosphingolipids,
and glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins.
,
Our histological studies focus on N-glycosylation. It has been elucidated
by numerous studies that N-glycans partake in a multitude of essential
biological procedures within cancer, such as inflammation, immune
surveillance, intercellular adhesion, cell-matrix interactions, intercellular
and intracellular signaling, as well as cellular metabolism.
−
Moreover, abnormal glycoprotein functions have been manifested in
a diverse range of cancers, including liver cancer, gastric cancer,
and ovarian cancer.
−
Specifically, as the disease progresses from cirrhosis
to early- and late-stage Hepatocellular Carcinoma,
Helicobacter pylori
glycans exhibit significant upregulation
in fucosylation and sialylation, with concurrent increases in the
expression of high-mannose glycans;
in
gastric cancer, homologous genes regulating high-mannose synthesis
(e.g., ALG3) are found to modulate the immune microenvironment by
altering the glycosylation of immune checkpoint molecules.
However, the systemic role of high-mannose modification
in NPC-distinct from these epithelial tumorshas not been fully
clarified, leaving a gap in our understanding of NPC-specific glycosylation
dysregulation. Thus, a comprehensive characterization of NPC using
quantitative glycoproteomic approaches will help to investigate the
role of NPC-specific protein glycosylation.
In this study, we
measured N-glycosylation levels in 17 NPC tumor
tissues and 7 noncancerous nasopharyngeal tissues (NT) via liquid
chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, while
also assessing site-specific glycosylation.
Significant alterations in glycosylation were observed in NPC compared
to the NT group. In addition, through the employment of clustering
and subclustering techniques, we delved into the disparities in glycosylation
levels among diverse immune subtypes. It was discovered that there
exists a distinct difference in the glycosylation type between the
groups with high and low immune infiltration. Protein expression generally
plays a significant role in regulating numerous cellular processes.
However, the precise function of glycosylation modifications in relation
to protein expression remains elusive.
Consequently, we conducted a comprehensive analysis to prognosticate
the crosstalk between glycosylation levels and protein expression
in NPC. We detected an association between the types of glycans and
protein expression, and furthermore, we predicted immunotherapeutic
targets related to glycosylation. Overall, the aforesaid findings
imply that protein glycosylation plays a significant role in NPC.
Furthermore, this data set offers a rich foundation for subsequent
studies focused on developing therapeutic interventions for nasopharyngeal
carcinoma.

Glycoproteomic Profiles of NPC
In this study, we extracted
proteins from 17 untreated nasopharyngeal carcinoma tumor tissues
as well as 7 normal nasal mucosal epithelial tissue samples, trypsinized
them, and performed label-free proteome quantification and mass spectrometry-based
intact N-glycoproteomic analysis to study the glycoproteomic profile
of NPC.

2,689,783 Total spectra, 1,208,390 Matched spectra, 102,104 Peptides,

proteins (
Figure S1A
). Most peptides carry
2–3 charges, and the peptide segments were distributed across
7–20 amino acids (

distribution of identified protein molecular weights across all size

The overall profile of the identified intact
glycopeptides filtered
by database searches against the data was analyzed as follows: there
were 6219 identified intact glycopeptides, 2098 Comparable intact
glycopeptides, 946 Identified proteins and 379 comparable proteins
(
Figure S1D
). Most
peptides in the data were distributed in the 7–20 amino acid
range, with their distribution consistent with common norms of enzymatic
digestion and MS fragmentation; notably, the peptide length distribution
identified by mass spectrometry satisfied quality control criteria
(
Figure S1E,F
). In addition, of the identified
N-glycosylation sites, 442 were newly discovered in this project,
and another 1120 N-glycosylation sites have been annotated in the
UniProt database (
Figure S1G
). N-glycosylation
has a specific residue pattern, i.e., a specific motif, which occurs
on the side-chain amino group of asparagine (N, Asn), succeeded by
any amino acid except proline (Pro, P), and the third residue is serine
(Ser, S), threonine (Thr, T), or cysteine (Cys, C), of which Cys is
rare. Key adjacent residues of this particular motif may determine
the interaction between the enzyme and the substrate and other potential
biological functions.
Motif analysis
of N-glycosylation sites via the MoMo tool revealed sequence patterns
consistent with the N–X­(^P)–S/T consensus motif (
Table S2
), confirming the reliability of the
identified modification sites.
Glycosylation modifications are governed by diverse factors, encompassing
peptide synthesis, protein folding, the localization and competitive
interactions of glycosyltransferases, the localization and abundance
of glycosidases, and transmembrane trafficking. Consequently, glycosylated
proteins may exhibit glycan heterogeneity at identical modification
sites.

Given that immune escape is a key hallmark of NPC
progression,
and immune checkpoint molecules (e.g., PD-L1) are critical mediators
of this process. We next focused on glycosylation changes of immune
checkpoint-related proteins to identify potential immunotherapeutic
targets. Among these, PD-L1 (encoded by CD274) was selected for in-depth
analysis, as it is a well-validated target in cancer immunotherapy
and its glycosylation status has been linked to treatment response
in multiple tumors. Currently, PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies represent
one of the most prominent targets in cancer immunotherapy. These anti-PD-1/PD-L1
agents function through inhibiting the interaction between PD-1 expressed
on activated T lymphocytes and PD-L1 localized on tumor cells, thereby
recovering the immune system’s tumor recognition and elimination
capacity. Notably, PD-L1’s N-glycosylation is critical for
maintaining its stability, which could prevent PD-L1 from being degraded
by the proteasome. In tumor cells, unglycosylated PD-L1 is prone to
phosphorylation by glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β),
which further triggers β-transducin repeat-containing protein
(β-TrCP)-mediated polyubiquitination and ultimately results
in its degradation through the 26S proteasome; in contrast, glycosylation
at sites such as Asn192, Asn200, Asn219 enhances PD-L1 stability,
allowing it to persist stably on the cell surface and continuously
exert immunosuppressive effects.
Given
the established role of PD-L1 glycosylation in enhancing protein stability,
facilitating PD-1/PD-L1 recognition, and promoting immune evasion,
we further investigated the correlation between
PD-L1 protein expression and its glycosylation patterns. We found
that the 192nd asparagine residue of PD-L1 in tumor tissues was modified
with varying degrees of processing of high-mannose glycans. Among
these, the levels of two intact glycopeptides, PD-L1_192_N2H7 and
PD-L1_192_N2H6, were notably elevated in NPC relative to NT (
p
< 0.05). Furthermore, PD-L1_192_N2H6 showed a robust
positive correlation with PD-L1 expression (
r
= 0.722,
p
= 0.001) (
Figure
C). This further supports the functional relevance of high-mannose
glycosylation in NPC immune escape.
Subsequently, to identify
the key enzymatic regulators of PD-L1
N-glycosylation, we analyzed the correlation between PD-L1 expression
and glycosyltransferase levels. Our analysis revealed a significant
positive correlation between MANEA and both PD-L1 expression (
p
< 0.05) and high-mannose glycosylation (
p
< 0.01). These findings suggest that MANEA may regulate PD-L1
protein expression through direct modulation of its high-mannose glycans.

Therefore, integrating our findings that MANEA
knockdown impairs
NPC cell proliferation and migration, regulates pathways governing
cell cycle, immune response, and energy metabolism, and interacts
with the PD-L1 axis to modulate immune evasion through high-mannose
glycosylation, we believe that MANEA plays a multifaceted and pivotal
role in NPC progression. It not only drives the malignant biological
behaviors of tumor cells but also bridges glycosylation remodeling
with immune microenvironment dysregulation, thereby emerging as a
potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt tumor
growth and restore antitumor immune surveillance.
Discussion
Within this research, a total of 6,219 intact
N-linked glycopeptidescorresponding
to 946 glycoproteins in totalwere successfully identified
and quantified using glycoproteomics approaches, with samples including
17 NPC and 7 NT. Significantly up-regulated and down-regulated intact
glycopeptides in NPCs differed in terms of glycans distribution and
pathways associated with the corresponding glycoproteins compared
to the NT. The flowchart of this study is presented in
Figure
.
5
Flowchart.
We discovered that the up-regulated glycopeptides
primarily originated
from those implicated in extracellular matrix organization, the regulation
of insulin-like growth factor (IGF) transport and uptake by insulin-like
growth factor binding proteins (IGFBPs), the development of nasopharyngeal
carcinoma, and integrin-mediated cell adhesion. This result corroborates
previous observations that emphasize N-linked glycosylation’s
regulatory role in cell adhesion and proliferation.
,
It is also important to acknowledge the limitations of this
work.
First, the number of samples analyzed is relatively small, and the
amount of tissue available for glycopeptide enrichment is insufficient;
second, there is interindividual heterogeneity in tumor tissues. These
factors together lead to only minor significant changes in N-glycopeptide
levels. Additionally, radiomics data were extracted from the clinical
examination results of referred patients, but not all patients underwent
PET-CT examinations, which to some extent compromised the reliability
of the conclusions. Nevertheless, proteomic analysis has identified
several proteins in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) samples. Among
them, some were previously recognized as promising biomarkers (e.g.,
JCHAIN, DAPL1), and others as potential therapeutic targets (e.g.,
WFDC2, BPIFA1, SP2). This finding indicates that the sample preparation
workflow based on surface digestion, combined with retrospective analysis
of tissue samples, can generate high-quality and reliable data.
Change in glycan types may be associated with cancer progression.
In the current study, a substantial percentage
of the upregulated glycopeptides were characterized by high-mannose
glycans, with Paucimannose and Sialylated glycans subsequent to them
in terms of abundance. Increased high-mannose glycans affect protein
function and promote cancer progression. Tumor-related signaling pathways
(e.g., EGFR/PI3K) may simultaneously upregulate the transcription/translation
of these proteins and the expression of glycosyltransferases (e.g.,
MANEA for high-mannose), leading to parallel increases in protein
abundance and glycosylation. For some proteins (e.g., PD-L1, as discussed
earlier), glycosylation can enhance protein stability and reduce degradation.
In this case, increased glycosylation may indirectly promote higher
protein expression, rather than the reverse.
Our experiments
found that the effects of MANBA and EDEM3 on the
proliferation and migration of nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells were
not as significant as those of MANEA (
Figure S4A–F
). But MANBA has been found to be associated with the risk of colorectal
cancer in the Swedish population.
,
More interestingly,
however, overexpression of EDEM3 stimulates mannose pruning in total
glycoproteins as well as misfolded glycoproteins, and EDEM3 likely
acts as a processing α1,2-mannosidase in vivo.
This seems to conflict with the results of high-mannose
modification in cancer,
which could be
that it plays a different function in tumors. Past studies have also
found that high EDEM3 expression in prostate tumors may additionally
show a positive correlation with unfolded protein response genes in
patients, whose expression can be triggered by radiation exposure.
Notably, EDEM3 overexpression drives radioresistance in prostate cancer
cells, and this phenotype is mitigated by EDEM3 depletion.
Therefore, glycosyltransferases associated with
high-mannose may play a crucial role in tumors. In addition to the
prominent increase in high-mannose glycans, we observed a relative
decrease in sialylated structures on down-regulated glycopeptides.
While the expression of canonical sialyltransferases was not significantly
altered in our data set, this shift may reflect a broader reprogramming
of the glycosylation pathway, where increased flux toward high-mannose
processing limits the substrate availability for complex sialylation.
The functional implications of reduced sialylation in NPC and the
potential post-translational regulation of sialyltransferases remain
to be fully elucidated and represent a valuable avenue for future
research.
Alterations in the glycosylation of tumor cell surface
glycoproteins
impact the ability of immune cells to recognize and eliminate tumor
cells. As a key glycosylation-related enzyme, MANEA may modulate the
stability, ligand affinity, and signaling activity of immune checkpoint
molecules by reshaping the glycosylation patterns of tumor cell surface
glycoproteins. This regulatory effect, in turn, influences immune
cell function and tumor immune escape, providing a theoretical basis
for the development of MANEA-based immunotherapeutic strategies. In
addition, linear regression modeling revealed correlations between
glycopeptide profiles and protein expression levels, suggesting that
N-linked glycosylation may regulate protein stability and thereby
influence protein expression. For instance, in our cohort, a notable
association was observed between the HexNAc(2)­Hex
glycan structure at position 192 of PD-L1 and PD-L1 protein
expression. This finding aligns with broader evidence that PD-L1 exists
in diverse molecular formsincluding soluble fragments (e.g.,
≈25 kDa extracellular domain cleaved by proteases) and distinct
glycan types (such as sialylated, fucosylated, or high-mannose)each
with unique implications for immune evasion. Specifically, high-mannose
glycan types like HexNAc(2)­Hex
may enhance
PD-L1 stability by reducing proteasomal degradation and strengthen
its binding to PD-1, thereby reinforcing T cell suppression; sialylated
PD-L1, on the other hand, can evade recognition by anti-PD-L1 antibodies
(e.g., atezolizumab) or interact with Siglec receptors on immune cells
to promote an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Soluble PD-L1 fragments
may even act as “decoys” to sequester PD-1, impairing
T cell activation without direct tumor cell contact. As a key glycosidase,
MANEA is hypothesized to regulate these PD-L1 variants: aberrant MANEA
activity may stabilize high-mannose PD-L1 glycan types, promote the
release of soluble fragments (by altering glycan-mediated protease
resistance), or modulate sialylation/fucosylation to enhance immune
evasion. This suggests that targeting MANEA could normalize PD-L1’s
glycan type profile and fragment dynamics, reversing its immune-evasive
effects. A promising combinatorial strategy for NPC involves co-targeting
MANEA and PD-L1. MANEA inhibitors boost therapeutic efficacy by reducing
PD-L1’s high-mannose glycans to promote antibody binding and
T cell recognition, while anti-PD-L1 antibodies directly disrupt immune
checkpoint interaction. This rationale aligns with reports that targeting
glycosyltransferases (e.g., FUT8, MGAT5) enhances immune checkpoint
inhibitor efficacy,
,
positioning MANEA/PD-L1 co-inhibition
as a novel approach to circumvent immunotherapy resistance.
Currently, research on MANEA as an immunotherapeutic target remains
in its early stages, with a lack of clinical data supporting direct
immunotherapeutic interventions targeting MANEA. Future research can
be carried out in the following directions: first, conduct in-depth
investigations into the expression patterns, functional roles, and
regulatory mechanisms of MANEA across different tumor types; second,
develop MANEA-specific inhibitors or activators and systematically
evaluate their effects on tumor immune responses; third, explore synergistic
treatment strategies through combining MANEA-directed therapies with
current immunotherapeutic modalities (such as immune checkpoint inhibitors
and cancer vaccines) for enhanced overall treatment outcomes.
In this study, we comprehensively characterized the glycoproteomics
of NPC through the analysis of a large-scale clinical cohort, presenting
the first report of quantitative glycopeptides in NPC to date. Currently,
the first-line treatment for NPC consists of radiation and chemotherapy.
Moreover, the ongoing development of novel therapies has achieved
breakthroughs in immune checkpoint therapy for recurrent or metastatic
NPC cases. Our pivotal findings may furnish new approaches to stratify
NPC patients and present new options for future development of diagnostics
and therapeutics for
cancer-specific glycan
types associated with NPC progression and aggressiveness,
glycoproteome isoforms, and
the interplay between glycosylation and protein expression.
In summary, this study illustrates that glycoproteomics can broaden
our insights into NPC by uncovering aberrant biological processes
not captured by our prior proteomic analyses. Furthermore, this study
provides a rich resource for translational research in oncology and
the broader medical fraternity.
Conclusions
Our study established the first large-scale
quantitative intact
N-glycoproteome data set for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. We sequenced
17 nasopharyngeal carcinoma tissue samples and 7 noncancerous tissues
and found that high-mannose modified proteins dominate the glycoproteins
of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. We confirmed that proteins modified with
high-mannose dominate the glycoprotein alterations in nasopharyngeal
carcinoma, affecting not only tumor cell proliferation, migration,
and invasion, but also immune escape mechanisms. Importantly, this
work confirms for the first time that the glycosidase MANEA associated
with high-mannose processing regulates the biological behavior of
nasopharyngeal carcinoma by regulating NPC cells’ high-mannose
glycosylation and is closely related to the expression of PD-L1 protein,
likely affecting immune escape in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. These
findings provide new targets for future immunotherapy strategies.
